The problem

The physical world does not always provide a reliable position.

Modern autonomy and digital experiences increasingly depend on knowing where a system or person is. Yet many environments are GPS-denied, degraded, dynamically changing, poorly mapped, or simply too costly to instrument with dedicated positioning hardware.

Public & commercial venues

People struggle to find their way.

In airports, hospitals, shopping centres and large mixed-use venues, visitors lose time finding stores, services and destinations — adding demand on staff and friction to every visit.

Autonomous systems

Machines lose reliable positioning.

Drones, ground vehicles and robots operate in places where satellite positioning is jammed, degraded or unavailable, and conventional navigation cannot be relied upon.

How GeoSnap solves it

A spatial intelligence layer for the real world.

GeoSnap turns visual information from existing cameras and sensors into spatial understanding — a complementary layer that adds resilience where conventional positioning falls short, rather than replacing the systems already trusted.

Visual localisation

Determines position from what existing cameras and sensors see — indoors and in GPS-denied environments.

Contextual understanding

Learns the layout, features and meaning of a specific space — not just coordinates on a map.

Natural-language guidance

Answers environment-specific questions and guides people and systems in plain language.

By learning the unique characteristics of an environment, GeoSnap becomes a digital expert for that space.

What is GeoSnap?

GeoSnap is a vision-based spatial intelligence technology that helps people and machines understand where they are, navigate with confidence and interact with their surroundings. It learns the unique characteristics of each environment and becomes a digital expert for that space — helping determine location, guide navigation and answer questions about the surroundings.

Finding your way through a complex place is rarely just about knowing your location. A visitor needs to understand what is around them, where they want to go and what might be useful along the way. An autonomous system faces a similar challenge, but in environments where GPS may be unavailable, signals may be unreliable and conditions can change continuously.

GeoSnap builds an understanding of the environment from visual information and uses it to determine where it is and what is happening around it. It does not need the environment to remain exactly as it was when it was first seen. A familiar place can change — new buildings, different layouts, vegetation, lighting or temporary obstacles — while GeoSnap continues to reason about the space and recognise meaningful changes.

Solutions

One spatial intelligence platform. Many physical-world applications.

GeoSnap adapts the same underlying technology to different operational challenges — from autonomous systems operating without reliable GNSS to large venues helping people navigate complex spaces.

Defence & Robotics

Autonomous and secure navigation in defence-critical applications

In defence operations, UAVs and ground vehicles increasingly depend on satellite positioning that can be jammed, spoofed, degraded or denied in contested environments — leaving autonomous systems unable to establish where they are or continue their mission. The same challenge extends to dismounted personnel, where smart-glass systems can add visual danger recognition and spatial awareness in the field. GeoSnap provides a vision-based positioning layer that keeps these systems oriented when conventional navigation cannot be relied upon.

Continuous operation in GPS-denied environments

Enables autonomous systems to position themselves globally with less than 10 m accuracy in GPS-denied environments, maintaining the continuity of operation.

Signal-free, privacy-preserving localisation

Enables autonomous defence systems to locate and navigate without transmitting or relying on external signals — reducing electronic detectability and protecting operational privacy.

Agriculture

Autonomous agricultural field robotics

Companies developing autonomous robots for weeding, crop monitoring, spraying and seeding need reliable navigation under crop and tree canopies — in orchards, vineyards and other environments where GPS is weak or intermittent. GeoSnap provides vision-based localisation that keeps these robots operating where satellite positioning cannot be relied upon.

Stereo-vision targeting demonstration, BOTany Robotics.

GeoSnap is collaborating with BOTany Robotics with the aim of integrating vision-based localisation into their autonomous field platform — enabling reliable row-following and precise targeting between crops where GPS is weak, obstructed or intermittent.

Construction & Infrastructure

Large-scale construction and infrastructure projects

Construction and engineering companies delivering major infrastructure — railways, roads, bridges, utilities and energy facilities — increasingly rely on repeated drone surveys to monitor construction progress, site conditions and assets. GeoSnap turns that imagery into consistent spatial understanding, so repeated surveys can be aligned and compared reliably even where GPS is obstructed or imprecise.

Drone Delivery & Logistics

Autonomous drone delivery for last-mile logistics

Drone delivery operators need backup visual localisation when GPS or GNSS is degraded, unavailable or unreliable — particularly in dense urban areas, between buildings and close to infrastructure. GeoSnap provides a vision-based positioning layer that supports mission continuity through these conditions.

Theme Parks

Hyperlocal navigation for large visitor attractions

Theme-park operators manage large, complex environments where infrastructure-free hyperlocal navigation can be built into existing apps — helping visitors find rides, facilities and services faster, and improving the overall guest experience.

About me

When GPS or GNSS is unavailable or unreliable, people and autonomous systems lose one of their most critical capabilities: knowing where they are, and how to get where they need to be.

I am building the next generation of vision-based navigation — a working technology, not just a research concept, that provides a reliable additional layer of positioning when conventional navigation cannot be relied upon. It learns from the environment more like humans do, adapting to new places, changing seasons and lighting, and recognising locations even when they look different over time.

The goal is not to replace GPS or GNSS, but to add positioning and navigation capability when it becomes unreliable, unavailable or denied — across autonomous systems, drones, construction, agriculture, logistics, smart buildings and other complex environments.

Experience

  • Over five years across AI, autonomous systems, robotics, computer vision and machine learning, in both industry and academic research.
  • Secured up to £350,000 in combined UK and EU funding for the University of Surrey and my research laboratory.
  • Contributed, in an industry research role, to collaborations with Lenovo and to seed-funding initiatives backed by Aramco.
